summary: Specifies SHA-224, a 224-bit one-way hash function. It is based on SHA-256 but starts from a different initial value and truncates the result to 224 bits, giving a hash size that matches the key strength of some other algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: SHA-224 is a one-way hash function: it turns a message of any length into a 224-bit fingerprint, and no practical way is known to work backwards from the fingerprint to the message. It is the same machinery as SHA-256 with a different starting point and a shorter answer, which gives 112 bits of security strength, the level NIST guidance expects when a 112-bit key algorithm is in use.

questions: how is sha-224 different from sha-256
subtitle: A 224-bit hash function made by starting SHA-256 from different numbers and dropping the last word.

tldr.problem: NIST guidance on cryptographic key management talks about five levels of security, and there was no one-way hash function for the 112-bit level, so a suite that needed 112 bits of security had nothing to use for hashing.
tldr.mechanism: SHA-224 runs the SHA-256 compression function from a different set of eight 32-bit starting values, then keeps only the first seven 32-bit words of the 256-bit result.
tldr.outcome: The memo publishes the specification and the three test vectors for the Internet community, and gives the ASN.1 object identifier that protocols such as CMS use to name the algorithm.

today: RFC 3874 is an Informational memo published in September 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes SHA-224 as specified by NIST in the FIPS 180-2 Change Notice of February 28, 2004, and publishes the specification and the test vectors for the Internet community.

sections.title: What SHA-224 Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3874 specifies a 224-bit one-way hash function called SHA-224. One-way hash functions are also known as message digests. SHA-224 is based on SHA-256, the 256-bit one-way hash function already specified by NIST in FIPS PUB 180-2. The National Institute of Standards and Technology announced the FIPS 180-2 Change Notice on February 28, 2004, which specifies the SHA-224 one-way hash function.

The reason SHA-224 exists is a gap in key management guidance. NIST is developing guidance on cryptographic key management and published a draft for comment. Five security levels are discussed there: 80, 112, 128, 192 and 256 bits of security. One-way hash functions were available for all of these levels except one, and SHA-224 fills that void. It provides 112 bits of security, which the memo calls the generally accepted strength of Triple-DES.

The memo gives two pieces of guidance on choosing between hashes. When selecting a suite of cryptographic algorithms that all offer 112 bits of security strength, SHA-224 is an appropriate choice for the one-way hash function. When terseness is not a selection criterion, the use of SHA-256 is a preferred alternative. Roughly the same amount of effort is consumed to compute a SHA-224 or a SHA-256 digest, so the smaller one costs nothing to run. Some usage environments are sensitive to every octet that is transmitted, and there the digest value provided by SHA-224 is 4 octets smaller, which is what matters. The use of a different initial value ensures that a truncated SHA-256 message digest value cannot be mistaken for a SHA-224 message digest value computed on the same data.
sections.plainLanguage: There was one hole in the list of security strengths that NIST's key management guidance talks about: 112 bits. SHA-224 is the hash function that fills it, and it is meant to sit alongside a key algorithm of the same strength. It runs at about the same speed as SHA-256 and gives back a value that is four bytes shorter.

sections.title: How SHA-224 Is Computed
sections.content:
SHA-224 may be used to compute a one-way hash value on a message whose length is less than 2^64 bits. It makes use of SHA-256. To compute a one-way hash value, SHA-256 uses a message schedule of sixty-four 32-bit words, eight 32-bit working variables, and produces a hash value of eight 32-bit words.

The function is defined in the exact same manner as SHA-256, with two exceptions. The first is the initial hash value. For SHA-224, the initial hash value of the eight 32-bit working variables, collectively called H, consists of the following eight 32-bit words in hex: H_0 = c1059ed8, H_1 = 367cd507, H_2 = 3070dd17, H_3 = f70e5939, H_4 = ffc00b31, H_5 = 68581511, H_6 = 64f98fa7 and H_7 = befa4fa4.

The second exception is the result. SHA-224 makes use of the first seven 32-bit words in the SHA-256 result and discards the remaining 32-bit word. The final value of H is therefore H_0 || H_1 || H_2 || H_3 || H_4 || H_5 || H_6, where || denotes concatenation.
sections.plainLanguage: Computing a SHA-224 value takes two steps. The same work as SHA-256 is done, but the eight 32-bit working variables start from different numbers. The 256-bit answer that comes out is then cut down by throwing away the last 32-bit word, leaving 224 bits.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The memo gives three test vectors so that an implementation can check that it computes the same values as everyone else.

The first hashes the 24-bit ASCII string abc, which is the binary string 01100001 01100010 01100011. The SHA-224 hash value in hex is 23097d22 3405d822 8642a477 bda255b3 2aadbce4 bda0b3f7 e36c9da7.

The second hashes the 448-bit ASCII string abcdbcdecdefdefgefghfghighijhijkijkljklmklmnlmnomnopnopq. The SHA-224 hash value in hex is 75388b16 512776cc 5dba5da1 fd890150 b0c6455c b4f58b19 52522525.

The third hashes the binary-coded form of the ASCII string made of 1,000,000 repetitions of the character a. The SHA-224 hash value in hex is 20794655 980c91d8 bbb4c1ea 97618a4b f03f4258 1948b2ee 4ee7ad67.
sections.plainLanguage: Three known inputs and their correct answers are given, so a programmer can check an implementation against them. The three inputs are the letters abc, a longer standard test string, and a million copies of the letter a.

sections.title: The Object Identifier
sections.content:
NIST has assigned an ASN.1 object identifier for SHA-224. Some protocols use object identifiers to name one-way hash functions, and CMS, defined in RFC 3852, is one example. Implementations of such protocols that make use of SHA-224 MUST use the following object identifier.

id-sha224  OBJECT IDENTIFIER  ::=  { joint-iso-itu-t(2)
            country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101)
            csor(3) nistalgorithm(4) hashalgs(2) sha224(4) }
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols that need to name a hash function in their data use a dotted number for each one. The number that stands for SHA-224 is given here, and implementations MUST use that one when they need it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
One-way hash functions are typically used with other cryptographic algorithms, such as digital signature algorithms and keyed-hash message authentication codes, or in the generation of random values. When a one-way hash function is used together with another algorithm, the other algorithm may require a hash function with a particular number of bits of security. If a message is being signed with a digital signature algorithm that provides 128 bits of security, then that signature algorithm may require a one-way hash algorithm that provides the same number of bits of security. SHA-224 is intended to provide 112 bits of security, which is the generally accepted strength of Triple-DES.

The author states that no independent assertion of the security of this one-way hash function is intended for any particular use, and adds that as long as SHA-256 provides the expected security, SHA-224 will also provide its expected level of security.
sections.plainLanguage: Hashes are rarely used on their own. They are paired with signature algorithms and message authentication codes, and those may insist on a hash of a matching strength. The memo says its author makes no claim about SHA-224 for any particular use, only that it inherits its security from SHA-256.

items.title: Different starting point
items.text: A different initial value ensures that a truncated SHA-256 digest cannot be mistaken for a SHA-224 digest computed on the same data.

items.title: Four octets shorter
items.text: Some environments are sensitive to every octet transmitted, and SHA-224 gives a digest that is 4 octets smaller.

items.title: When to pick which
items.text: SHA-224 suits a suite offering 112 bits of security strength. When terseness is not a criterion, SHA-256 is the preferred alternative.
